SOAH DOCKET NO. 473-26-16349
PUC DOCKET NO. 59475

INTERVENORS CHARLES E. AND CHERYL L. RAEKE’S
INITIAL BRIEF
I.  INTRODUCTION
Intervenors Charles E. Raeke and Cheryl L. Raeke (collectively, "Raeke" or "Intervenors") own Tract 2642 in Williamson County, Texas. Proposed Link F41 of Oncor Electric Delivery Company LLC and LCRA Transmission Service Corporation's (collectively, "Applicants") Bell County East Switch to Big Hill Substation 765-kV transmission line project crosses directly through Tract 2642, placing a permanent high-voltage corridor beside the Raeke family residence and occupied outbuildings.
Intervenors submit this Initial Brief. The record demonstrates that Link F41 is not the route best supported by the statutory routing factors under PURA Section 37.056(c) and 16 Tex. Admin. Code Section 25.101. The Commission should select an alternative route that avoids or materially minimizes impacts to Tract 2642.
In the alternative, if the Commission approves Link F41, Intervenors request binding mitigation conditions, including minimum setback requirements, pre- and post-construction water-well monitoring, pre-construction threatened-species survey, and meaningful construction notice to Intervenors.
II.  PROCEDURAL BACKGROUND
Applicants filed a Joint Application seeking to amend their Certificates of Convenience and Necessity ("CCN") to construct the Bell County East Switch to Big Hill Substation 765-kV transmission line project. SOAH Order No. 6, adopted April 20, 2026, governs this proceeding.
On April 27, 2026, Intervenors timely filed their Motion to Intervene and obtained full party status. On May 13, 2026, Intervenors timely filed their written direct testimony (Sworn Written Testimony of Charles E. and Cheryl L. Raeke, admitted as Exhibit 23) and Statement of Position opposing Link F41.
On May 15, 2026, Intervenors served their First Requests for Information ("RFIs") on Applicants, seeking among other things: Applicants' PURA Section 37.056(c) routing-factor analysis and scoring matrices (RFI 1-2); habitable-structure inventories within 300, 500, and 1,000 feet of the centerline of each filed route (RFI 1-3); route-paralleling tabulations (RFI 1-7); side-by-side comparative cost analyses including cost per habitable structure avoided (RFI 1-12); environmental-constraints and biological analyses (RFI 1-5); prudent-avoidance, EMF, and visual-impact analyses (RFI 1-6); cumulative-impact studies (RFI 1-17); and comparable transmission-easement compensation data, stigma and marketability analyses, and settlement and award data (RFIs 1-24, 1-25, 1-26, 1-29, 1-30).
On June 3, 2026, Intervenors filed their Witness List and Exhibit List, designating Charles E. Raeke, Cheryl L. Raeke, and realtor Wade Gordy as witnesses. 
The Hearing on the Merits was conducted June 8-12, 2026.

III.  Applicants' Failure to Respond to Discovery — Intervenors Are Prejudiced
Intervenors served their First Requests for Information on May 15, 2026. Under SOAH Order No. 6, responses were due within seven working days of service. Applicants have not served responses to Intervenors' RFIs. That failure materially prejudices Intervenors' ability to fully develop and brief the record on the statutory routing-factor analysis, comparative route data, and damages.
The unanswered RFIs address information uniquely within Applicants' possession and directly material to the Section 37.056(c) analysis:
RFI 1-2: Applicants' PURA Section 37.056(c) routing-factor scoring matrices, criteria weights, and route rankings -- the proprietary analysis underlying Applicants' assertion that F41 is the preferred route.
RFI 1-3: Habitable-structure inventories within 300, 500, and 1,000 feet of the centerline of each filed route -- data essential to comparing structure-proximity impacts across competing alternatives.
RFI 1-7: Route-paralleling tabulation showing miles and percentage of each filed route paralleling existing utility ROW, roadways, or property lines -- the statutory factor most strongly favoring alternatives to F41.
RFI 1-12: Comparative cost analysis, including cost per habitable structure avoided -- the benchmark for testing whether F41's cost profile justifies its structure-proximity impacts.
RFI 1-5: Environmental-constraints maps and biological, archaeological, and floodplain analyses for routes including Link F41 -- necessary to assess the threatened-species concerns on Tract 2642.
RFI 1-6: Prudent-avoidance, EMF, and visual-impact analyses -- necessary to assess Applicants' compliance with the prudent-avoidance standard applicable to the Raeke residence.
RFI 1-17: Cumulative-impact studies for the Ronald Reagan Parkway, Schwertner pipeline, I-14 corridor, and area substations -- necessary to quantify the compounded burden on Tract 2642 and the Jarrell corridor.
RFIs 1-24, 1-25, 1-26, 1-29, 1-30: Comparable 345-kV+ transmission easement compensation data, EMF/health/property-value studies, stigma and marketability analyses, and settlement and award data -- all material to a complete record on damages if Link F41 is approved.
Intervenors reserve all rights and objections arising from Applicants' failure to respond to discovery. To the extent the record is incomplete because Applicants withheld responsive information, that incompleteness should be construed against Applicants. The Commission should not reward a party's discovery non-compliance with the benefit of an undeveloped record. Intervenors reserve the right to supplement this brief if and when Applicants produce RFI responses.
IV.  Governing Legal Standard
PURA Section 37.056(c) requires the Commission to evaluate a CCN amendment application on the basis of the "best interests of landowners and the general public," with consideration of, among other factors: feasibility of the proposed route; effect on the environment and welfare of the affected area; minimization of impacts on habitable structures and use of existing rights-of-way; cost, including cost per habitable structure avoided; and prudent-avoidance principles regarding EMF exposure. 16 TAC Section 25.101 implements these criteria.
The burden of proof rests with Applicants to demonstrate that the proposed route is the route best supported by these statutory factors. That burden is not met by silence on material criteria -- including routing-factor scoring, habitable-structure comparisons, paralleling analysis, and cost-per-structure metrics -- that Applicants were ordered or obligated to disclose and failed to produce. Intervenors submit that on the record before the Commission, Applicants have not carried their burden of proving that Link F41 is the route best supported by the Section 37.056(c) factors as applied to Tract 2642.

V.  Link F41 Is Not the Route Best Supported by the Statutory Factors
A.  Habitable Structures -- F41 Performs Worst of All Routes
The Raeke family residence and occupied outbuildings are located on or immediately adjacent to the Link F41 centerline as it crosses Tract 2642. The proposed 765-kV ROW would place permanent transmission structures within 300 feet of the Raeke family home. Charles and Cheryl Raeke testified to these facts in their Sworn Written Testimony (Ex. 23), admitted into evidence at the hearing.
The statute and implementing rules identify minimization of impacts on habitable structures as a primary routing criterion. Link F41 fails this criterion on Tract 2642 more severely than any other filed route. To Intervenors' knowledge, no other competing link places a 765-kV line within 300 feet of an occupied residence. Applicants refused to produce their PURA Section 37.056(c) scoring analysis (RFI 1-2) and habitable-structure inventory (RFI 1-3), preventing Intervenors from confirming the full magnitude of this differential. That evidentiary gap is Applicants' burden, not Intervenors'.
Multiple additional occupied structures on and adjacent to Tract 2642 fall within the 500-foot and 1,000-foot prudent-avoidance bands along the F41 corridor, compounding permanent exposure to EMF, audible noise, and visual impact. The filed alternative routes travel along existing utility, roadway, or field-edge corridors with materially fewer habitable structures in proximity.
B.  Failure to Parallel Existing Rights-of-Way
Link F41 cuts a new corridor across Tract 2642. It does not follow any existing utility transmission line ROW, roadway, or established property boundary through the Raeke property. Charles and Cheryl Raeke testified that they never granted, negotiated, or were approached about a prior transmission easement on Tract 2642 before this proceeding. (Ex. 23.) The aerial and parcel maps of Tract 2642 admitted as Exhibit 3 demonstrate that F41 imposes a greenfield corridor crossing on an intact, contiguous agricultural tract.
The statutory preference for routing along existing ROW and compatible land-use corridors is a fundamental criterion under PURA Section 37.056(c) and 16 TAC Section 25.101(b)(3)(B). Applicants refused to produce the route-paralleling tabulation (RFI 1-7), preventing a quantitative comparison. However, the record evidence, including the certified aerial and parcel maps (Ex. 3) and Intervenors' route comparison demonstrative (Ex. 23), establishes that filed alternatives make substantially greater use of existing ROW and compatible corridors than Link F41. A route that avoids new corridor incursions into occupied agricultural tracts while paralleling existing ROW is by definition better supported by the statutory factors than Link F41.
C.  Prudent Avoidance and EMF
Link F41 routes a 765-kV transmission line directly beside the Raeke family residence. This fails the prudent-avoidance standard applicable to occupied structures. The Raeke family would live and work within the permanent shadow of a 765-kV line indefinitely, with ongoing daily exposure to EMF, audible conductor noise, and the visual impact of transmission towers -- none of which can be mitigated away once the line is constructed.
Applicants' prudent-avoidance, EMF, and visual-impact analyses (RFI 1-6) were not produced. To the extent Applicants argue at any stage that Link F41 satisfies prudent-avoidance standards, that argument is unsupported by any evidence in this record that was produced to or tested by Intervenors.
D.  Cost Per Habitable Structure Avoided -- An Unreasonable Trade
The cost-per-habitable-structure-avoided metric exists to test whether marginal engineering cost savings justify the harm to occupied structures. Link F41 places the Raeke residence within 300 feet of a 765-kV line. Applicants refused to produce any comparative cost analysis or the cost-per-structure-avoided data (RFI 1-12) that would permit the Commission to evaluate this trade-off.
Charles and Cheryl Raeke testified that any marginal cost savings Oncor might assert do not justify placing a 765-kV line next to their home and occupied structures, and that the economic burden imposed on Tract 2642 far exceeds any nominal engineering cost differential. (Ex. 23.) On the record as developed, the Commission cannot find that the cost-per-structure-avoided ratio for Link F41 is reasonable or consistent with the Legislature's direction to minimize impacts on habitable structures.
E.  Environmental Constraints
Charles and Cheryl Raeke observed on Tract 2642 wildlife consistent with Texas Horned Lizard habitat -- a Texas state-listed threatened species. (Tex. Parks & Wild. Code Section 68.002.) The property also contains drainage features and low-lying areas that may implicate floodplain constraints along the F41 corridor. (Ex. 23.)
Applicants' environmental-constraints maps and biological, archaeological, and floodplain analyses (RFI 1-5) were not produced. Intervenors cannot confirm whether Applicants' environmental analysis for Link F41 is accurate or complete. The presence of threatened-species habitat and drainage features on Tract 2642, unchallenged by Applicants' evidence, weighs in favor of an alternative route.
F.  Cumulative and Co-Located Impacts
The Jarrell corridor surrounding Tract 2642 already carries a disproportionate and growing infrastructure burden. The Ronald Reagan Parkway (FM 1105) right-of-way extension has imposed additional encumbrances on this corridor, including a significant taking from the adjacent Rundberg tract (Tract 2641.1). The Jarrell-Schwertner Water Supply Corporation perpetual pipeline easement adds further encumbrance. I-14 corridor development and area substation activity continue to increase the infrastructure load in this area.
Link F41 stacks a new 765-kV transmission corridor on top of existing and planned infrastructure concentrations, compounding rather than distributing the regional infrastructure burden. Charles and Cheryl Raeke testified that this compounded burden accelerates the diminution in value of their property beyond what the transmission line alone would cause. (Ex. 23.) Applicants' cumulative-impact studies (RFI 1-17) were not produced. The Commission should require Applicants to demonstrate that F41's cumulative impacts on the Tract 2642 corridor are no greater than those of competing alternatives before approving this route.
G.  Effect on Community Values, Agricultural Use, and Land
Tract 2642 is an active agricultural property supporting a goat operation with an agricultural tax exemption in place. The proposed F41 corridor bisects the tract, disrupting cultivation, grazing, and field operations across the centerline strip and access easement. Permanent tower structures and access-road placement would impair the Raeke family's ability to use and manage the property as a functioning agricultural operation.
One water well on Tract 2642 is at risk from construction vibration, equipment traffic, and permanent EMF exposure. Loss of this water source would directly affect agricultural and domestic operations.
Additionally, Tract 2642 suffered a documented market-value loss directly attributable to the pendency of the Link F41 application. In early 2026, the Raeke family listed the Tract 2642 residence for sale. A buyer entered a real estate sales contract and passed all option periods without issue. On May 22, 2026 -- the scheduled closing date -- the buyer received Oncor's utility-disclosure packet identifying the proposed 765-kV Link F41 corridor and terminated the contract on that basis. No other basis for termination was identified. The home was relisted; no subsequent buyer has expressed interest, due directly to market stigma from the proposed transmission line. As a direct consequence, the Raeke family was compelled to obtain mortgage financing to close on a new home purchase they had planned to fund from the proceeds of the Tract 2642 sale.
Realtor Wade Gordy, testifying at the hearing, confirmed that buyer aversion to high-voltage transmission lines is real, quantifiable, and material to the marketability of Tract 2642. This documented real-world market reaction is uniquely attributable to Applicants' selection of Link F41 over available alternatives and constitutes direct evidence of harm to community values and land under PURA Section 37.056(c).
VI.  Summary -- Statutory Factor Comparison
The following table summarizes Intervenors' analysis of each PURA Section 37.056(c) factor. Because Applicants refused to produce responsive data in answer to Intervenors' RFIs, entries marked (*) reflect Intervenors' assessment from the available record evidence; those figures should have been supplied by Applicants.


* Intervenors' assessment from available record evidence; precise figures withheld by Applicants in response to RFIs 1-2, 1-3, 1-5, 1-6, 1-7, 1-12, 1-17.
VII.  Alternative Relief -- Binding Mitigation Conditions
In the event the Commission approves Link F41, Intervenors request the following binding mitigation conditions be imposed as part of any CCN order:
                  Minimum setback requirements for tower structures from the Raeke residence and occupied outbuildings, to the extent engineering permits;
Pre-construction survey and post-construction monitoring of the water well on Tract 2642 at Applicants' sole expense, with a binding obligation to restore or replace the well if construction activity or ongoing operations cause damage or interference;
Pre-construction survey for Texas Horned Lizard and harvester ant colonies within the F41 corridor on Tract 2642, with appropriate avoidance or mitigation measures required;
Access road placement that minimizes disruption to the goat operation and agricultural use;
Restoration of all disturbed agricultural land to pre-construction condition at Applicants' sole expense upon completion of construction; and
Written notice to Intervenors' counsel of record no fewer than 30 days prior to the commencement of any construction activity on or adjacent to Tract 2642.
VIII.  Preservation of the Record on Damages
Intervenors recognize that compensation for the taking of an easement is determined in a subsequent condemnation proceeding under Tex. Prop. Code Ch. 21, not in this docket. Intervenors nonetheless submit the following for completeness of the administrative record and preservation of all rights in any condemnation proceeding that may follow a CCN grant on Link F41.
The record in this docket documents the following categories of compensable injury to Tract 2642:
Easement strip value: The per-acre or per-linear-foot value of the 765-kV transmission easement, to be established by a qualified condemnation appraiser using comparable 345-kV+ transmission easement transactions. (See RFIs 1-24, 1-26, unanswered; Exhibits 16, 17.)
Remainder damages -- structure proximity: The Raeke residence lies within 300 feet of the proposed centerline. Structure-proximity harm of this magnitude is peculiar to this remainder, not a generalized community effect barred by State v. Schmidt, 867 S.W.2d 769 (Tex. 1993), and constitutes compensable severance damage.
Remainder damages -- market stigma and loss of marketability: The documented May 22, 2026 contract termination -- the buyer's express reason being receipt of Oncor's utility-disclosure packet identifying Link F41 -- provides direct market evidence of value loss caused by the proposed line. Buyer aversion to high-voltage transmission facilities is compensable when supported by market evidence. Heddin v. Delhi Gas Pipeline Corp., 522 S.W.2d 886 (Tex. 1975). Realtor Wade Gordy's testimony and the documented relisting with no buyer interest corroborate this market reaction.
Remainder damages -- agricultural use impairment: Disruption of the goat operation, loss of unrestricted field access across the easement corridor, and permanent impacts on agricultural operations constitute compensable severance damage to the remainder.
Remainder damages -- water well: Risk to and potential loss of the domestic and agricultural water well on Tract 2642 is a compensable element of the taking.
Forced mortgage costs: The Raeke family's documented forced mortgage obligation, resulting directly from the Oncor-disclosure-driven termination of their pending sale, is a cognizable element of consequential damages in connection with the condemnation.
These elements are supported by the testimony of Charles E. Raeke, Cheryl L. Raeke, and realtor Wade Gordy, and by the admitted exhibits, including Exhibits 3, 4, 22, and 23. Intervenors reserve the right to retain a qualified condemnation appraiser to prepare a full appraisal of damages in any subsequent Tex. Prop. Code Ch. 21 proceeding.
IX.  Prayer for Relief
For all the foregoing reasons, Intervenors Charles E. Raeke and Cheryl L. Raeke respectfully request that the Commission:
DENY Applicants' request to amend their CCNs to construct the Bell County East Switch to Big Hill Substation 765-kV transmission line on Link F41 as it crosses Tract 2642, and REQUIRE selection of an alternative route that avoids Tract 2642 or materially reduces impacts on habitable structures, existing agricultural use, and the Raeke family's water supply;
In the alternative, IMPOSE the binding mitigation conditions set forth in Section VII of this Brief as a condition of any CCN order approving Link F41;
PRESERVE for the administrative record all testimony and exhibits concerning damages to Tract 2642 -- including the documented May 22, 2026 sale failure, market stigma, forced mortgage obligation, agricultural use impairment, and water well risk -- for use in any subsequent condemnation proceeding; and
GRANT Intervenors such other and further relief to which they may be justly entitled.

engineering cost savings justify the harm to occupied structures. Link F41 places the Raeke
residence within 300 feet of a 765-kV line. Applicants refused to produce any comparative
cost analysis or the cost-per-structure-avoided data (RFI 1-12) that would permit the
Commission to evaluate this trade-off.
        Charles and Cheryl Raeke testified that any marginal cost savings Oncor might
assert do not justify placing a 765-kV line next to their home and occupied structures, and



                Intervenors Charles 13. and Chcryl L. Racke -· Initial Brief   ·   Page 4 of 9
 that the economic burden imposed on Tract 2642 far exceeds any nominal engineering cost
differential. (Ex. 23.) On the record as developed, the Commission cannot find that the
cost-per-structure-avoided ratio for Link F41 is reasonable or consistent with the
Legislature's direction to minimize impacts on habitable structures.

        E. Environmental Constraints
        Charles and Cheryl Raeke observed on Tract 2642 wildlife consistent with Texas
Horned Lizard habitat -- a Texas state-listed threatened species. (Tex. Parks & Wild. Code
Section 68.002.) The property also contains drainage features and low-lying areas that may
implicate floodplain constraints along the F41 corridor. (Ex. 23.)
        Applicants' environmental-constraints maps and biological, archaeological, and
floodplain analyses (RFI 1-5) were not produced. Intervenors cannot confirm whether
Applicants' environmental analysis for Link F41 is accurate or complete. The presence of
threatened-species habitat and drainage features on Tract 2642, unchallenged by
Applicants' evidence, weighs in favor of an alternative route.

        F. Cumulative and Co-Located Impacts
       The Jarrell corridor surrounding Tract 2642 already carries a disproportionate and
growing infrastructure burden. The Ronald Reagan Parkway (FM 1105) right-of-way
extension has imposed additional encumbrances on this corridor, including a significant
taking from the adjacent Rundberg tract (Tract 2641.1). The Jarrell-Schwertner Water
Supply Corporation perpetual pipeline easement adds further encumbrance. I-14 corridor
development and area substation activity continue to increase the infrastructure load in this
area.
        Link F41 stacks a new 765-kV transmission corridor on top of existing and planned
infrastructure concentrations, compounding rather than distributing the regional
infrastructure burden. Charles and Cheryl Raeke testified that this compounded burden
accelerates the diminution in value of their property beyond what the transmission line
alone would cause. (Ex. 23.) Applicants' cumulative-impact studies (RFI 1-17) were not
produced. The Commission should require Applicants to demonstrate that F41's
cumulative impacts on the Tract 2642 corridor are no greater than those of competing
alternatives before approving this route.

        G. Effect on Community Values, Agricultural Use, and Land
        Tract 2642 is an active agricultural property supporting a goat operation with an
agricultural tax exemption in place. The proposed F41 corridor bisects the tract, disrupting
cultivation, grazing, and field operations across the centerline strip and access easement.
Permanent tower structures and access-road placement would impair the Raeke family's
ability to use and manage the property as a functioning agricultural operation.
         One water well on Tract 2642 is at risk from construction vibration, equipment
traffic, and permanent EMF exposure. Loss of this water source would directly affect
agricultural and domestic operations.
         Additionally, Tract 2642 suffered a documented market-value loss directly
attributable to the pendency ofthe Link F41 application. In early 2026, the Raeke family
listed the Tract 2642 residence for sale. A buyer entered a real estate sales contract and

       the buyer received Oncor's utility-disclosure packet identifying the proposed 765-kV Link
       F41 corridor and terminated the contract on that basis. No other basis for termination was
       identified. The home was relisted; no subsequent buyer has expressed interest, due directly

       had planned to fund from the proceeds of the Tract 2642 sale.
              Realtor Wade Gordy, testifying at the hearing, confirmed that buyer aversion to
       high-voltage transmission lines is real, quantifiable, and material to the marketability of
       Tract 2642. This documented real-world market reaction is uniquely attributable to
       Applicants' selection ofLink F41 over available alternatives and constitutes direct evidence
       of harm to community values and land under PURA Section 37.056(c).

                   VIII. PRESERVATION OF THE RECORD ON DAMAGES
         Intervenors recognize that compensation for the taking of an easement is determined in a
subsequent condemnation proceeding under Tex. Prop. Code Ch. 21, not in this docket. Intervenors
nonetheless submit the following for completeness of the administrative record and preservation
of all rights in any condemnation proceeding that may follow a CCN grant on Link F41.
The record in this docket documents the following categories of compensable injury to Tract 2642:
   •   Easement strip value: The per-acre or per-linear-foot value of the 765-kV transmission
       easement, to be established by a qualified condemnation appraiser using comparable 345-
       kV+ transmission easement transactions. (See RFIs 1-24, 1-26, unanswered; Exhibits 16,
       17.)
   •   Remainder damages -- structure proximity: The Raeke residence lies within 300 feet of
       the proposed centerline. Structure-proximity harm of this magnitude is peculiar to this



                       Intervenors Charles 13. and Chcryl L. Racke -· Initial Brief   ·   Page 7 of 9
        remainder, not a generalized community effect barred by State v. Schmidt, 867 S.W.2d
       769 (Tex. 1993), and constitutes compensable severance damage.
   •   Remainder damages -- market stigma and loss of marketability: The documented May 22,
       2026 contract termination -- the buyer's express reason being receipt of Oncor's utility-
       disclosure packet identifying Link F41 -- provides direct market evidence ofvalue loss
       caused by the proposed line. Buyer aversion to high-voltage transmission facilities is
       compensable when supported by market evidence. Heddin v. Delhi Gas Pipeline Corp.,
       522 S.W.2d 886 (Tex. 1975). Realtor Wade Gordy's testimony and the documented
       relisting with no buyer interest corroborate this market reaction.
       Remainder damages -- agricultural use impairment: Disruption of the goat operation, loss
       ofunrestricted field access across the easement corridor, and permanent impacts on
       agricultural operations constitute compensable severance damage to the remainder.
       Remainder damages -- water well: Risk to and potential loss of the domestic and
       agricultural water well on Tract 2642 is a compensable element of the taking.
       Forced mortgage costs: The Raeke family's documented forced mortgage obligation,
       resulting directly from the Oncor-disclosure-driven termination oftheir pending sale, is a
       cognizable element of consequential damages in connection with the condemnation.
    These elements are supported by the testimony of Charles E. Raeke, Cheryl L. Raeke, and
realtor Wade Gordy, and by the admitted exhibits, including Exhibits 3,4,22, and 23. Intervenors
reserve the right to retain a qualified condemnation appraiser to prepare a full appraisal of damages
in any subsequent Tex. Prop. Code Ch. 21 proceeding.
